newsitem.title: Italy: U.S. says there is no automatic right to be fed.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says there is no automatic right to be fed.

text.p: Wrangling over the aims of a U.N. food summit burst into the open on Sunday when the United States disputed the right to be fed and several Catholic and Moslem states reaffirmed their opposition to population controls.

In a written reservation to a declaration on hunger adopted at the World Food Summit, Washington said that achieving the right to adequate food was "a goal or aspiration" and not an international obligation on governments.

The five-day summit, which ended on Sunday, was sponsored by the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organisation (FAO) and has secured a non-binding international commitment to work to halve the number of the world's hungry to around 400 million by 2015.

It adopted by acclamation at its outset a non-binding Declaration on World Food Security which reaffirms in its opening paragraph "the right of everyone to have access to safe and nutritious food consistent with the right to adequate food and the fundamental right of everyone to be free from hunger".

"In joining consensus on this and other paragraphs...the United States does not recognise any change in the current state of conventional or customary international law regarding rights related to food," the U.S. reservation said.

"The United States believes that (this) is a goal or aspiration to be realised progressively but does not give rise to any international obligations nor diminish the responsibility of national governments towards their citizens," it said.
But in the hall where the summit took place, South Africa threw its weight behind calls by many African and other Third World nations to establish food as a basic human right.
"The hungry, wherever they may be, have a right to be fed," Deputy President Thabo Mbeki told the closing session.

The U.S. government expressed concern during more than two years of negotiations on the summit documents that a "right to food" could expose rich countries to law suits and trade complaints from the developing world.
The U.S. reservation also said Washington had not signed up to a target by the summit that countries should provide 0.7 percent of their annual economic wealth in development aid.
The United States provides just under one percent of its economy in aid but has traditionally refused to enshrine a specific goal.
Critics says the share of foreign aid in America's economy is one of the smallest in the industrialised world.
The U.S. declaration was among written reservations or interpretations lodged by 15 delegations, organisers said.
Others, including the Vatican, Argentina and several Moslem states, raised strong objections to references in the summit texts to population and family planning policies.

The plan of action at the food summit adopts a passage from the 1994 Population Conference in Cairo which committed nations to promoting primary health care and reproductive health services for all, especially the poor.
The Vatican and many developed countries clashed bitterly at the Cairo conference over wording.
The Vatican's reservation said references to family planning and reproductive health should not be seen as a change in the Roman Catholic Church's opposition to artificial birth control.
Argentina said policies aimed at stabilising populations should not interfere with ethical and religious values.
Iran and the United Arab Emirates both made clear they would intepret the documents in accordance with Islamic law.
Nigeria went further, saying it objected "strongly" to references to "appropriate population policies, programmes and family planning services" without directly excluding abortion.
The package of reservations also contained objections by Burundi, Libya, Iraq and Sudan to international sanctions that they say deprive their populations of food.
Burundi, hit by regional sanctions after a coup this year, dismissed a summit document call to "refrain from unilateral measures" as a euphemism, saying such actions should be banned.
